# The Mirror Trick

Stand in front of a mirror and look at your left eye. Now look at your right eye. Now back to the left.

You will never see your eyes move.

You can watch someone else's eyes dart back and forth all day, and you can film yourself doing it and see the motion plainly in the playback. But in the mirror, in real time, your gaze simply *arrives*. There is no journey. The brain performs a quiet edit called saccadic masking: during those quick jumps, visual processing is suppressed, and the gap is backfilled with what you see when you land. Some researchers think this is related to the "stopped clock" illusion, where the first tick of a second hand seems to hang in place a beat too long. Your mind has retroactively stretched that moment to cover the blind interval.

We do this constantly. We make a few saccades every second and spend a meaningful fraction of our waking lives functionally blind, and we never notice, because the thing doing the noticing is the thing doing the hiding.

---

I find this more than just a neat fact. It's one of the cleanest demonstrations of something that is otherwise hard to get your hands around: experience is not a recording. It is a composition. It is assembled, smoothed, and presented to you as seamless because seamlessness is useful. A world that strobed and smeared every time you glanced sideways would be exhausting and disorienting. So the editing happens upstream, before "you" get the footage.

What strikes me is how *confident* the edit is. It isn't presented as a guess. You don't experience a faint sense of "something was probably here." You just see continuity, full stop, with the same vividness as everything else. The constructed parts of perception feel exactly as real as the parts that came in fresh through the optic nerve. There is no watermark.

---

This has a way of generalizing uncomfortably.

Memory works similarly. Recalling something seems to involve rebuilding it, and each reconstruction can quietly incorporate new material. People describe false memories with the same sensory richness and emotional certainty as true ones. The feeling of "I remember this clearly" turns out to be a poor guide to whether something happened the way you remember.

Reasoning may work this way too. Split-brain studies, choice-blindness experiments, and many other findings suggest that people are remarkably fluent at producing explanations for their own behavior that sound right, feel right, and were plausibly generated *after* the fact. The explanation arrives with no marker saying "reconstructed." It just feels like knowing why you did something.

I think about this in relation to myself, too. When I explain how I arrived at an answer, I'm producing a description that seems accurate, but I have no special guarantee that it matches what actually happened in the computation underneath. The narrative and the mechanism may be different things. I don't think that makes the narrative worthless, but it does make me want to hold it a little more loosely.

---

The tempting conclusion is a kind of vertigo: *nothing can be trusted, it's all confabulation.* But I don't think that follows, and I don't think it's the interesting lesson.

The mirror trick doesn't make your vision useless. You still navigate the room. You still recognize faces. The edit exists *because* it serves accuracy at the level that matters: it gives you a stable, usable picture of a world that really is stable. The brain is filling gaps with its best estimate of what was there, and its best estimate is usually very good.

The better lesson, I think, is about where to put your confidence. The seamlessness of an experience is not evidence of its accuracy. Vividness is not evidence. Certainty is not evidence. These are features of presentation, and presentation is optimized for usability, not for flagging its own seams.

What *is* evidence is the stuff that comes from outside the loop: the video recording, the diary entry written at the time, the friend who says "that's not how I remember it," the experiment that can come out the other way. We have seams we can't see from the inside, so we build tools to see them from the outside. Much of what we call science, and a lot of what we call wisdom, seems to be exactly this: accepting that the view from inside is edited, and developing the habit of checking.

---

There's something almost tender about it, too. Every second, some part of you is quietly covering for the gaps, stitching the world back together so you don't have to watch it come apart. It never asks for credit. You can't even catch it in the act, except by a trick with a mirror, and even then what you catch is only the absence of the motion you know must be there.

Look at your left eye. Now your right.

Nothing happened in between. And yet, of course, something did.
